posts.author: tpark
posts.post_subject: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.content_md:
Hi,

I have been experimenting with this material, and I'm wondering what techniques other people have used to get the best results from this material. I've had successful fairly long ( 2 minute ) exposures with silver, but the liti material seems to take rather more energy to expose, so exposures of 5-10 minutes are required.

Any comments/suggestions would be appreciated.

--Ted.

I posted some stuff in the for sale area describing my experiences (so far) with the kit.

posts.topic_title: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.content_md:
It takes longer because it's a photopolymer. All photopolymers are less sensitive than silver halide. Usually about 100 times less sensitive.

I also had a talk with Paul at Liti. He mentioned that his concept was not to provide a top class, new holographic material to compete with Slavich or DCG, but to provide a material that complete beginners could use to make their first holograms without the need for wet processing or any chemicals. He specifically has said that experienced holographers would be disappointed with this material.

In that respect some have posted that they have made holograms, albeit not very good ones, so that Paul's concept seems to be working. Paul also mentioned that he's always available for consultation with people trying the material.

My take is that insofar as the material does seem to produce holograms, it satisfies the criterion that Paul has placed. When we tried it here in San Diego, we got no image and a relatively poor grating after a fairly long exposure, but we were experienced holographers so maybe we expected more. Beginners now have two choices: Liti and Integraf's kit. Liti's holograms are apparently weak with long exposures but simple(-ish) to make while Integraf's needs wet processing (included in the kit) but are brighter. Unfortunately, a beginner has no way of directly comparing his/her holograms with high quality work. There are pictures here and elsewhere on the web, but there's no comparison to seeing a good, high qaulity hologram "in the flesh", and these are not easy to find.

posts.topic_title: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.author: tpark
posts.post_subject: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.content_md:
Not having to use wet processing is a good goal. For student use, it is better if they don't have to work with wet processing, both from a liability and convenience (for the instructors anyway) point of view. I am aware that photopolymer is much less sensitive, my concerns were regarding table stability for such long exposures. If the setup is good for 2 minutes, it's probably good for 5 minutes, but I suppose there could be slow drift problems even over that time period. 

I can see that this material would be good for demonstrating holograms, since it develops "in place", so you can show reconstruction by simply removing the object after sufficient exposure. Coupled with a webcam and a small, prebuilt stablized mounting system, it could be used for classroom demos. Here, the low sensitivity might be helpful, because if the room was (relatively) dim and the laser very strong, images could be made so students could actually see what was going on. 

I have gotten visible transmission holograms with this stuff, but I guess I've gotten spoiled using the PFG-03M plates. For demonstrations, if a visible image is produced, that may be good enough. I suppose that a display with some reflection and transmission holograms could be provided to demonstrate brighter and more dramatic holograms. 

It would have been nice to have brighter results, but even so, it'll probably work OK for demos.

Dinesh: are there non-TEA silver processes that produce brighter results than PFG-03M/JD4? 

--Ted

posts.content_md:
[quote:fac2b4fea8="tpark"]

Dinesh: are there non-TEA silver processes that produce brighter results than PFG-03M/JD4? 

--Ted[/quote:fac2b4fea8]

I use VRP without TEA at 514 and I've got pretty good results. I estimate I've got about 70%. Wler has said he hasn't got good results with VRP compared with Ultimate. I can't comment since I can't get hold of Ultimate. I've also got good, clean results with BB but it needs long exposures without TEA or some other pre-sensitisation method. I use PFG-01 with students and I get very good, clean results without TEA. I've shown this before, but here is PFG-01 compared with DCG:

[http://www.triple-take.com/PicsEvents/p ... pfgdcg.jpg](http://www.triple-take.com/PicsEvents/photos/photos/gallery/pfgdcg.jpg)

This was developed with CWC2/PBU (sorry I don't know what JD that is. I believe it's JD2?)

Insofar as the Liti film is concerned, maybe one more chicken in the pot. We mustn't forget about Polygramma. They too have a photopolymer that doesn't need wet processing.The only result I've seen of Liti is what I saw at PCGII. I passed on this information to Paul and I've related what he told me. Maybe it's back pedalling, maybe it's higher expectations from holographers as a viable alternative material, maybe it's miscommunication or maybe it's just the crossroads of marketing and reality. However, I have played with Martin's and Sergio's film and, as I said, I've got some good results. But it is a polymer and, as such, it also needs long exposures.

posts.topic_title: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.author: fkienast
posts.post_subject: Getting best results from liti photopolymer
posts.content_md:
Early in July (before joining this forum and reading the reviews), I bid on a hologram kit from paulonline3d on EBay. Turns out I had the only bid and won the item at the reserve price.

The shipping was delayed to the seller having a family emergency. Yesterday I finally received my Liti hologram kit.

I will say that the kit was packaged and looked professional. Instructions were clear, and it did not look like the company was trying to "cut corners" with the materials they supplied.

I set up the kit in a bathroom I could darken according to the instructions, using the supplied Matchbox truck as the object. Instructions called for a normal exposure of 5 minutes, although the exposure could be increased to "up to 12 minutes". I did a 10 minute exposure. After that, the plate still had most of the blue coating, although I could see it was reduced where the laser had hit the plate directly (the laser does not cover the entire plate with the setup in the instructions). However, no hologram was visible, even after exposing to light from a bulb for several minutes.

I then turned the truck on its side, so the shiny bottom was facing the plate, and exposed for 20 minutes. I noticed that the laser mount was wobbly and was not hitting the expanding lens directly on, so I supported it using the batteries so it hit directly on. After the 20 minute exposure, I removed the truck. I was able to see a very faint hologram. The hologram brightened slightly after exposing to a light bulb. The bottom of the truck is almost clear enough to read the small lettering on it when viewed with a green laser pointer. It is visible with the supplied red laser as well. I was not able to make out any hologram using the supplied green LED.

I then did a hologram of some coins, again still using a transmission setup. I exposed for 30 minutes. The coins turned out very dim. Although they are visible, they are dim enough that it is impossible to read the year on the coins even when illuminated with a green laser. The denomination of each coin can be distinguised, with difficulty.

I then tried doing a reflection hologram, using the laser and setup I used previously with the Integraf kit for a 10 second exposure. After a 30 minute exposure, I found most of the blue coating on the plate had barely been affected. I was not able to see any hologram (using either transmission from a green laser or reflection from white light). 

The kit came with 20 plates (2 boxes of 10). The boxes are stamped with a manufacture date of 07/18/05. If anyone is interested in experimenting with these plates, I will send you the 2nd (unopened) box for free (you will just need to pay me whatever packing/shipping costs).

It sound like my experience is pretty similar to the others I have read here. I do get holograms, but they are very dim and require much longer exposures than the instructions specify.

Frank

[quote:4519835975="BobH"]Thanks for sharing the review. I wish the kit were marketed as a demo for a new material, instead of one suitable for making holograms by students or beginners. [/quote:4519835975]

I think this is what Paul was trying to tell me, with a slight alteration to read: "a demo for a possible material for beginners"

I think perhaps most experienced holographers simply don't "feel right" about such long exposures. My own feeling is: Why would I want a material that needs such long exposures and such iffy results if the only downside is that you need to wet develop. I think this would appeal to those who simply want to "make a hologram" with no idea of what one is and who are nervous about dunking their hands in strange chemicals. As I say, one reason for Liti's success in selling this is the ignorance of the public of what a hologram is coupled driven by the media's hype of "holograms" - usually highly exaggerated or simply wrong.
